papers.title: A Dual Soft Attention Network for Automatic Sleep Staging via Single-Lead Electrocardiogram Signals.
papers.abstract: Polysomnography (PSG) is the current gold standard for sleep monitoring; however, it is complex, burdensome, and costly. In contrast, commercial health monitoring devices, such as the Apple Watch, offer sleep scoring at a low cost over a few days. This paper proposes a dual-attention mechanism-based sleep staging method using single-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) signals, named SleepECGNet. The method extracts multi-scale features by employing convolutional kernels of different sizes, thereby capturing subtle details in the ECG signals. The model then integrates an SE module and a Luong attention-based encoder-decoder architecture to filter redundant information and dynamically focus on different sleep stages. Experiments were conducted using the HMC, MGH, and SHHS1 datasets for sleep staging tasks and the Apnea-ECG corpus was employed to execute transfer learning strategies directed at sleep apnea recognition. Comprehensive ablation experiments were conducted to verify the effectiveness of each component. Moreover, an analysis of sequence duration demonstrated that expanding the input timeframe directly improves classification outcomes.

papers.title: Language-supervised electrocardiogram interpretation with vision transformer.
papers.abstract:
PURPOSE: Most artificial intelligence models for electrocardiogram (ECG) interpretation rely on task-specific supervised learning, requiring dedicated labeled datasets for each diagnostic task and limiting scalability across diverse cardiac conditions. This study investigated whether vision-language learning from paired ECG recordings and summary reports could enable transferable ECG representations without task-specific supervised training.

METHODS: We developed ECG-VLM, a contrastive vision-language model consisting of a Transformer-based image encoder and a text encoder, trained on 800,034 paired 10-s ECG recordings and summary reports from the MIMIC-IV-ECG database. Cardiac condition detection was performed using natural-language prompts without condition-specific retraining or fine-tuning. Performance was evaluated on an internal test set and externally validated using the LSAS-ECG dataset (45,151 recordings) across 14 cardiac conditions, together with retrieval and subgroup analysis.

RESULTS: ECG-VLM achieved diagnostic performance across 14 cardiac conditions, with AUROC ranging from 0.679 to 0.981 on the internal test set and from 0.691 to 0.991 on external validation. Performance was strongest for rhythm abnormalities (mean AUROC 0.948 internally and 0.921 externally) and lower for morphological conditions. Compared with the previously reported signal-based ECG-CLIP framework, ECG-VLM achieved comparable performance for rhythm abnormalities while improving AUPRC for several morphological conditions. Performance remained broadly consistent across external validation and demographic and clinical subgroups.

CONCLUSION: These findings demonstrate the feasibility of vision-language supervision from paired ECG recordings and summary reports for learning transferable ECG representations without task-specific supervised training. This framework provides a basis for future extension of vision-language learning to ECG images encountered in routine clinical practice.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s13755-026-00482-7.

papers.title: Memristor-based echo state network for ECG classification: optimizing accuracy and efficiency with different architectures.
papers.abstract: Electrocardiogram (ECG) signal classification is a crucial task in automated cardiac monitoring and early disease detection. Conventional machine learning and deep learning methods often face challenges related to high computational costs, large data requirements and difficulty in handling real-time ECG analysis. In this work, we have proposed three memristor-based echo state network (MESN) models for ECG classification: (1) MESN, (2) Parallel MESNs (PMESN) with a classifier and (3) Attention-enhanced MESN (AMESN), where all three models employ artificial neural network (ANN) as a readout layer. These models leverage the property of an ESN to transform ECG signals into high-dimensional representations, thereby enhancing classification performance. The proposed models were evaluated on different benchmark ECG datasets: ECG200, ECG5000, ECGFiveDays, NonInvasiveFetalECGThorax1, NonInvasiveFetalECGThorax2, and TwoLeadECG. The results demonstrate that AMESN achieves the highest precision, recall, F1-score and overall accuracy particularly excelling in datasets with high intra-class variability. Whereas, PMESN improves robustness by leveraging multiple reservoir layers, while MESN provides a strong baseline with computational efficiency. These models are also compared with other state-of-the-art models and the analysis shows that AMESN achieves 1.92-13.39% higher accuracy, demonstrating superior performance. These findings highlight the potential of ESN as a lightweight yet powerful approach for ECG classification, making it suitable for integration into wearable and IoT-based healthcare systems.

papers.title: AI-based multimodal analysis of ECG and clinical data for evaluation for competitive sports participation: The VALETUDO trial.
papers.abstract:
AIMS: Pre-participation cardiovascular screening (PPS) is essential for preventing SCD in athletes, yet ECG interpretation requires expertise and remains resource-intensive. We aimed to evaluate the feasibility and diagnostic performance of a deep learning (DL) model for analysis of clinical data and resting 12‑lead ECG obtained during routine PPS in competitive athletes.

METHODS: In this prospective single center observational study, competitive athletes aged 18 to 60 years and undergoing routine PPS were enrolled. PPS included medical history, physical examination, resting and exercise ECG. Athletes were classified as fit or not fit for competitive sports according to clinical evaluation. Resting ECG and clinical variables were analyzed using a multimodal DL architecture. Model performance was assessed using stratified 10-fold cross-validation against PPS clinical classification.

RESULTS: A total of 526 athletes were enrolled (72% male, median age of 27 years (IQR: 20-41); 166 (32%) had a negative PPS result. The test setting (10-fold cross-validation), the model achieved moderate discrimination with an accuracy of 0.64 ± 0.08, SE 0.68 ± 0.15, SP 0.61 ± 0.17, F1-score 0.72 ± 0.1, PPV 0.80 ± 0.07, NPV 0.48 ± 0.12, AUC 0.72(0.66-0.78). Training performances reached accuracy of 0.70 ± 0.06, SE 0.73 ± 0.12, SP 0.67 ± 0.14, F1-score 0.77 ± 0.07, AUC 0.79 (0.74-0.83).

CONCLUSION: Automated DL-based analysis of 12‑lead ECG during PPS is feasible and showed encouraging diagnostic performance in competitive athletes. Although wider experience and external validation is required, AI-assisted multimodal ECG interpretation may represent a useful adjunct to physician assessment for cardiovascular risk stratification in sport screening programs.

papers.title: IoT-based ECG arrhythmia detection and classification model using an optimization based hybrid deep capsule stacked autoencoder.
papers.abstract: Heart disease is one of the most dangerous diseases, and it is getting worse in adults over the age of 40. Cardiac arrhythmia is defined as an irregular heartbeat, and quick diagnosis and treatment are critical for saving the lives of a huge population. Currently, the arrhythmia classification involves diverse challenges that limit the existing methodologies from attaining the desired results. Some of the major challenges involve signal quality issues, including noise and motion artefacts, class imbalance and dataset limitations, generalization issues due to context variability across patients, real-world deployment and clinical trust. Several methodologies have been introduced to date to focus on these critical issues, but most of them are unable to cover and address the issues altogether. This study offers a novel deep learning-based method for identifying and classifying arrhythmias as a remedy. First, the pre-processing step receives the input data, which includes body temperature, heart rate, blood oxygen level, and ECG signal. Pre-processing is done with min-max normalization and an enhanced wavelet Wiener filtering technique (UP_WWF) in this case. After pre-processing, the input is submitted to the feature extraction stage, which extracts significant features. Features are extracted using an adaptive dense convolutional osprey network where the osprey optimization algorithm is used to tune the parameters of the network for better feature discrimination. Finally, with the help of the extracted features, the various arrhythmia classes are classified using an attention-based deep capsule stacked autoencoder (Att_DCSAE). The proposed framework is evaluated using the MIT-BIH dataset for benchmarking, whereas the constructed combined ECG dataset includes ECG, heart rate, blood oxygen level, and body temperature measurements. The proposed approach resulted in an overall accuracy of 99.6% on the combined ECG dataset, signifying that it can be applied in hard real-world conditions. The study also shows significant improvements when evaluated on the MIT-BIH dataset with a total precision, recall, and F1-score values of 99.98%, 99.68% and 99.86%, resulting in the overall improvement of 0.6% precision, 0.08% recall, and 0.7% F1-score when compared with the latest techniques in the literature.

papers.title: A clinical decision support system for ECG diagnosis: Surpassing commercial standards through dual-stream feature fusion.
papers.journal: Computer methods and programs in biomedicine
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Automated electrocardiogram (ECG) interpretation is essential for clinical efficiency, yet many existing deep learning (DL) models are perceived as "black boxes" and lack direct benchmarking against established commercial standards. To foster clinician trust and support reimbursement justification, AI systems must demonstrate not only superior accuracy but also alignment with established clinical criteria.

METHODS: We proposed a Dual-Stream Signal Fusion Architecture that integrates latent spatio-temporal features from 21,799 raw 12-lead ECG waveforms (PTB-XL) with 148 expert-engineered clinical metrics extracted via commercial algorithms (PTB-XL+). The system was evaluated against the Marquette 12SL™ (12SL) commercial standard using the independent PTB-XL test set (Fold 10).

RESULTS: The proposed Hybrid Model achieved a Macro F1-Score of 0.851, significantly outperforming the commercial 12SL standard (0.812) and the waveform-only baseline (0.821). Notably, sensitivity for Myocardial Infarction (MI) improved by 10.8% relative to 12SL (0.72 vs. 0.65). Feature importance analysis confirmed that the model's decisions are clinically traceable, attributing 45% importance to QRS amplitude for Hypertrophy diagnosis, which aligns with Sokolow-Lyon criteria.

CONCLUSIONS: Our hybrid framework offers a superior, transparent, and robust standard for automated ECG interpretation. By outperforming clinical gold standards and providing physiologically sound reasoning, this work represents a step toward building the clinical evidence base for AI-based diagnostic support across diverse global populations; prospective, multi-site validation remains necessary before clinical deployment can be considered. The proposed framework is further distinguished by its modular design, which ensures adaptability across both resource-rich and resource-limited clinical environments.

papers.title: A novel method for analysis of transient morphological changes in quasiperiodic physiological signals and their neurogenic correlates.
papers.journal: Computer methods and programs in biomedicine
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVE: Transient changes in electrocardiographic (ECG) morphology often accompany fluctuations in heart rhythm and may provide clinically relevant information about cardiac function. However, conventional ECG visualization and analysis methods typically emphasize either waveform morphology or rhythm variability, making it difficult to assess their temporal interplay in long-term recordings and, consequently, to identify rhythm-related morphological changes and exploit their potential diagnostic value. This work presents a visualization framework for quasiperiodic physiological signals that enables simultaneous assessment of beat-to-beat morphological changes and rhythm dynamics in a single representation.

METHODS: The proposed method converts quasiperiodic signals into two-dimensional carpet plots. Characteristic events (e.g., ECG R peaks) are used to align consecutive signal segments, which are transformed into color-coded rows and stacked in chronological order. The resulting image preserves both the temporal evolution of signal morphology and variations in cycle duration. The method was evaluated using ECG recordings from multiple publicly available databases containing healthy subjects and patients with diverse cardiac abnormalities, as well as synchronized multimodal physiological recordings.

RESULTS: Carpet plots enabled rapid visualization of transient morphological changes alongside heart rate dynamics across recordings ranging from several minutes to hours. The representation highlighted clinically relevant phenomena, including ST segment alterations, QT interval variability, changes in T wave morphology, atrial fibrillation episodes, premature ventricular complexes, Wenckebach periodicity, and stress-test phase transitions. The image-based representation was also shown to be suitable for automated analysis using convolutional neural network feature extraction.

CONCLUSIONS: Carpet plots provide a compact representation of quasiperiodic physiological signals, jointly visualizing rhythm and morphology across long-term recordings. The proposed framework facilitates both expert interpretation and image-based computational analysis, offering a general approach for investigating transient physiological phenomena in ECG and other synchronized quasiperiodic signals.

papers.title: Adaptive graph convolutional neural network incorporating ECG for individualized motor imagery EEG classification.
papers.journal: Computer methods and programs in biomedicine
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVE: The recognition of motor imagery electroencephalogram (EEG) signals, which non-invasively capture the macroscopic electrical activity of the brain, is critical for medical rehabilitation and intelligent control. In these applications, reliable prediction is essential due to the safety risks associated with misclassification. However, existing methods often suffer from limited generalization in cross-subject scenarios caused by substantial inter-subject variability. To address this challenge, this work develops adaptive modeling strategies to improve robust cross-subject recognition performance.

METHODS: We propose a Hybrid Adaptive Domain Graph Convolutional Network (HAD-GCN) to enhance decoding performance through multi-level adaptability. At the spatial level, an adaptive generator synthesizes electrocardiogram (ECG) signals, which record the electrical activity of the heart, from EEG signals and concatenates them within a connected graph structure, thereby mitigating the limitations of non-invasive data acquisition. At the temporal level, an adaptive splitter selects the most suitable time-frequency domain processing method for each subject's signal and routes the data into the corresponding branches for feature extraction.

RESULTS: Accuracy and the Kappa coefficient, which are widely adopted in motor imagery research, are used as evaluation metrics. Cross-subject experiments conducted on the Mixed dataset and the BCI Competition IV-2a dataset achieve accuracies of 83.10% ± 6.54% and 74.81% ± 8.97%, respectively, with corresponding Kappa values of 0.778 ± 0.06 and 0.655 ± 0.09.

CONCLUSIONS: Experimental results demonstrate that HAD-GCN significantly improves cross-subject classification performance and prediction reliability while maintaining strong generalization capabilities. The proposed multi-level adaptive approach consistently enhances classification accuracy for individual subjects, highlighting its potential for practical applications in EEG-based technologies. Our code is available at https://github.com/chuanlaiair/HAD-GCN.

papers.title: A lightweight progressive residual convolutional network for interpretable arrhythmia classification.
papers.journal: Physical and engineering sciences in medicine
papers.abstract: Arrhythmia poses a serious threat to human health, necessitating research into automated diagnostic methods. Although advances have been made in arrhythmia classification using deep learning, existing models often suffer from high computational cost and poor interpretability, limiting their clinical applicability. To this end, this paper proposes a lightweight progressive residual convolutional attention network (DResCA). Through the synergistic design of stage-adaptive downsampling and channel attention, this network reduces parameter redundancy while enhancing deep ECG feature extraction. To enhance clinical interpretability, template matching and attention visualization are employed to reveal the key ECG regions underlying the model's diagnoses. Five-class classification experiments on the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database demonstrate that the model achieves 98.35% accuracy and 97.99% macro-F1 score while maintaining fewer parameters than mainstream deep learning models. These characteristics provide a practical technical pathway for real-time arrhythmia detection on wearable edge computing devices.

papers.title: Characterizing altered cardiac autonomic dynamics in psychotic disorders through multidomain heart rate variability analysis and deep learning.
papers.abstract: Recent developments in wearable devices have opened the possibility of heart rate variability (HRV), a quantitative measure of autonomic nervous system regulation, as a potential indicator for the early detection of psychiatric disorders. This study explores HRV for the detection of psychotic disorders by integrating multidomain HRV analysis with a hybrid deep learning technique. Polar H10 electrocardiogram device was employed to collect RR interval data from 30 patients diagnosed with either schizophrenia or bipolar disorder, and 30 similar age healthy controls, with a duration of approximately 1.5-2 h. HRV features, including time-domain, spectral, and nonlinear features such as the Poincaré plot and recurrence quantification analysis, were extracted from this publicly available dataset. Group-wise statistical comparisons between the healthy and the psychotic disorders were performed using the Mann-Whitneytest with a significance level of. HRV indices such as Mean NN intervals, SDNN, RMSSD, triangular index, Cardiac Vagal Index (CVI), Poincaré plot measures (SDand SD), Sample Entropy, and spectral power components (HF, LF, and total power), were significantly lower in the psychotic disorder group (), indicating attenuated autonomic modulation. All machine learning and deep learning models were conducted under a fully nested, subject-independent 54 cross-validation protocol in which minimum redundancy maximum relevance (mRMR) feature selection and hyper-parameter optimization were performed exclusively inside each outer training fold. Gradient Boosting achieved the highest subject level accuracy of, surpassing the best previously reported subject level accuracy ofon the same dataset. A hybrid CNN-BiLSTM-Attention network, applied to the same mRMR-selected features, achieved a competitive subject-level accuracy of. These results demonstrate that a rigorously nested evaluation combined with multidomain HRV features yields reliable subject-level discrimination and offers both performance and interpretability.

papers.title: HeartFusion: A Cross-Modality Transformer for Accurate Cardiovascular Disease Diagnosis and Severity Assessment.
papers.abstract: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) requires diagnostic models that can integrate complementary electrophysiological and anatomical information while also representing ordered disease severity. HeartFusion was developed as a mathematically informed cross-modality Transformer framework combining electrocardiogram (ECG) and cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Wavelet-derived ECG time-frequency representations were encoded with Cardioformer, MRI structure was encoded with TransUNet, and modality-specific embeddings were aligned in a shared latent space using cosine-similarity-based cross-modal attention. A transformer classifier performed diagnostic prediction, while an ordinal regression head modeled four ordered severity stages. Three controlled pseudo-paired benchmark cohorts were constructed from PTB-XL with ACDC (CVD-I), MIMIC-IV-ECG with CMRxRecon (CVD-II), and PTB-XL/MIMIC-IV-ECG with OCMR/Cardiac Atlas Project data (CVD-III). Source observations were partitioned before pseudo-pair construction to prevent cross-partition leakage, and five matched random seeds were used for evaluation. HeartFusion achieved diagnostic accuracies of 97.73%, 98.23%, and 98.02%, with AUC values of 98.12%, 98.76%, and 98.39% on CVD-I, CVD-II, and CVD-III, respectively. Severity staging achieved ordinal accuracies above 90%, with the best Cohen's kappa of 0.839 and MAE of 0.340. These findings support phenotype-level multimodal representation learning, while validation on genuinely patient-matched ECG-MRI cohorts remains necessary before clinical deployment.

papers.title: KDM-Net: a large-kernel and bi-mamba integrated network for 12-lead atrial arrhythmia classification.
papers.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Automatic recognition of atrial arrhythmias is important for early clinical screening and computer-aided diagnosis. Distinguishing atrial fibrillation from atrial flutter remains challenging because of their similar electrocardiographic manifestations andhigh risk of misclassification. This study aimed to develop an effective model for atrial arrhythmia classification with improved multi-lead feature utilization, long-range temporal modeling, and cross-patient generalization.

APPROACH: We propose KDM-Net, which takes12-lead electrocardiogram signals as input. The network employs a large-kernel K module to enhance the perception of waveform morphology and rhythm patterns, a D module to recalibrate and fuse multi-lead features, and a bidirectional Mamba-based M module tomodel long-range temporal dependencies. KDM-Net was evaluated on the combined CUSPH and PTB-XL dataset under an inter-patient protocol.

MAIN RESULTS: In five-fold cross-validation, KDM-Net achieved an average accuracy and F1-score of 96.04% and89.21%, respectively. On the independent patient-level test set, the accuracy and F1-score were 96.41% and 88.31%, respectively. On the CinC 2020 external test set, the model achieved an accuracy and F1-score of 91.14% and 80.41%, respectively. KDM-Netoutperformed several representative models in comparative experiments.

SIGNIFICANCE: KDM-Net effectively integrates multi-lead spatial information and long-range temporal dependencies, demonstrating strong recognition performance and promising cross-patientgeneralization. It provides an effective solution for the intelligent diagnosis of atrial arrhythmias.

papers.title: B-spline Kolmogorov-Arnold networks for interpretable semi-supervised ECG classification.
papers.abstract: This study investigates how Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) behave when combined with semi-supervised learning for single-lead ECG analysis. Three architectures are compared: a standard CNN-BiLSTM-Attention model (accurate but uninterpretable), a minimal KAN with a simple CNN front-end (ablation), and the proposed SE-MSC-KAN-CNN. The proposed model uses multi-scale depthwise convolutions, Squeeze-and-Excitation attention, BiLSTM, and a B-spline KAN head. Interpretability is evaluated in three ways: visualising learned B-spline functions, applying Grad-CAM to highlight important signal regions, and measuring how the splines change when fewer labels are used (spline drift). On the PhysioNet 2017 dataset (8528 recordings, four classes), the proposed model reaches 85.2% supervised accuracy (F1 = 0.851), outperforming the CNN baseline (83.1%) and matching much larger black-box models. With only 90% of the labels, it still achieves 85.1%. After training, we applied post-training TFLite INT8 conversion. Only the CNN-front-end KAN converted (measured size 422 KB). The proposed SE-MSC-KAN-CNN did not convert, because Bidirectional LSTM and custom attention lack TFLite kernels; its float32 footprint is about 9.8 MB (theoretical INT8 size about 806 KB). Classification metrics in this paper are float32; INT8 test accuracy was not measured. The spline drift metric summarises how KAN coefficients change under semi-supervised training; use as an on-device out-of-distribution detector is proposed but not validated here. These results show that competitive accuracy and inspectable KAN maps can be obtained in one hybrid architecture. Wearable deployment of the proposed SE-MSC-KAN-CNN is not yet achieved: TFLite INT8 conversion failed, and the present graph still requires float32 inference.

papers.title: STCP-Net: A few-shot learning approach based on spectral-temporal convolution and an improved prototypical network for ECG classification.
papers.abstract: To address the heavy reliance of deep learning models on manually labeled data in ECG classification, we need to tackle two major limitations. First, sample sizes are often limited in clinical settings, making data annotation costly and impractical. Second, existing few-shot learning methods still fall short in two key areas: 1) Existing strategies pay insufficient attention to rare arrhythmia types. This makes it difficult to effectively identify rare clinical cases. 2) Single feature representation fails to fully integrate the global frequency, local time-frequency, and semantic information of ECG signals. This results in incomplete feature representation. To overcome these challenges, we propose a novel few-shot learning method for ECG classification. In terms of feature extraction, a spectral-temporal convolution feature extractor is designed to precisely focus on the key information of ECG by efficiently integrating the global frequency, local time-frequency features and semantic information of the signal. Furthermore, with regard to classification, an improved prototypical network based on cross-class bias diminishing is developed to enhance the recognition performance for rare arrhythmia type samples. The experimental results show that the proposed method achieves significant classification performance across multiple public datasets, especially on Chapman, it attains an average accuracy exceeding 90% in the 2-way 1-shot and 2-way 5-shot tasks.

papers.title: Per-Class Conformal Risk Control for Multi-Label ECG Classification: Achieving Clinically-Justified False Negative Rate Guarantees.
papers.abstract: Automated electrocardiogram (ECG) classifiers require uncertainty procedures that address class-specific clinical risk in intrinsically multi-label data.Approach: We propose per-class risk-controlling prediction sets for multi-label ECG classification. For each diagnostic class, binary false-negative-rate (FNR) loss is calibrated with a one-sided exact-binomial upper confidence bound. The nine disease-specific targets are controlled simultaneously at 95% family-wise confidence using Bonferroni allocation. The final operating threshold is the more inclusive of the exact-binomial threshold and a conservative reference threshold derived from a concentration bound; this safeguard uses calibration data only and cannot weaken the exact guarantee.Main results: We evaluated the method on PTB-XL (21,388 retained recordings) and Chapman-Shaoxing (10,199 retained recordings), using a patient-disjoint PTB-XL split and fitting-partition-only normalisation. The proposed method met all 9/9 prespecified disease-specific FNR targets on held-out test sets and produced non-vacuous simultaneous exact-binomial guarantees for all nine targets; uniform standard conformal prediction met 5/9. Test FNR was 0.0% for myocardial infarction (exact 95% upper bound 0.35%, at 80.3% FPR), 1.0% for ST/T changes, and 0.3% for atrial fibrillation; the high-sensitivity operating point is purchased with substantially reduced specificity. Under PTB-XL-to-Chapman shift, macro class coverage fell from 94.3% to 45.5%, demonstrating that the guarantees do not transport without local recalibration.Significance: Exact-binomial per-class risk control provides a transparent high-sensitivity operating point for ECG triage while making its specificity, prediction-set-size, calibration-support, and exchangeability limitations explicit.&#xD.
